points: When: reduce read latency and DB load for hot, repeatedly-read data
Redis (rich data structures, persistence options) vs Memcached (simpler, pure in-memory)
Write-through: write to cache and DB together — consistent, slower writes
Write-back: write to cache first, flush to DB later — fast writes, risk of data loss
Write-around: write straight to DB, cache fills on next read
Eviction policies: LRU, LFU, TTL-based expiry
Cache stampede: many requests miss simultaneously and hammer the DB — mitigate with locking, request coalescing, or jittered TTLs
When: decouple producers/consumers, smooth traffic spikes, enable async processing
Kafka: high-throughput log, ordered within a partition, consumers track their own offsets, good for event streaming/replay
RabbitMQ: traditional broker, flexible routing (exchanges), good for task queues with complex routing
SQS: managed, simple, at-least-once delivery, good default when you don't want to run infra
Delivery guarantees: at-most-once vs at-least-once vs exactly-once (rare, expensive)
Idempotency matters on the consumer side once you accept at-least-once delivery
L4 (transport layer): routes by IP/port, fast, protocol-agnostic
L7 (application layer): routes by content (URL path, headers), enables smarter routing but adds latency
Sticky sessions: pin a client to one backend — simplifies stateful apps but hurts even load distribution
Algorithms: round robin, least connections, weighted, consistent hashing (good for cache-backed services to minimize reshuffling)
Health checks are what make failover actually work
SQL: strong consistency, joins, transactions — good when relationships and integrity matter
NoSQL: flexible schema, horizontal scale — good for high write throughput or unstructured/semi-structured data
Sharding: split data across nodes by a shard key — watch for hot shards and cross-shard queries/joins
Replication: leader-follower (read scaling, single write point) vs multi-leader/leaderless (write scaling, conflict resolution needed)
CAP theorem: under a network partition, choose Consistency or Availability — most real systems tune this per use case rather than picking one absolutely
Token bucket: tokens refill at a fixed rate, request consumes a token — allows bursts up to bucket size
Leaky bucket: requests processed at a fixed rate regardless of burstiness — smooths traffic, no bursts allowed
Fixed window: simple counter per time window — vulnerable to burst at window boundaries
Sliding window (log or counter): smooths the boundary problem, more accurate, more memory/compute
Where to enforce it: client, API gateway, or per-service — usually gateway for a shared limit
Strong consistency: every read sees the latest write — simpler mental model, costs latency/availability
Eventual consistency: replicas converge over time — higher availability, stale reads possible
Read-your-writes / session consistency: a middle ground often good enough for user-facing features
Tie back to CAP: the consistency model you pick is really a partition-tolerance trade-off decision
Blob/object storage (S3-style): flat namespace, great for large immutable files (images, videos, backups), not for frequent small updates
File storage: hierarchical, POSIX-like access, good for shared file systems (NFS/EFS)
Block storage: raw disk volumes attached to a single instance (EBS-style), used under databases/VMs
Metadata (structure, permissions, references) is usually stored separately from the raw blob itself
Elasticsearch/OpenSearch: inverted index for full-text search, good for relevance ranking, filtering, aggregations
Not a source of truth — usually synced from a primary DB via CDC or dual writes
Sharding + replicas same as other distributed stores — tune for read-heavy search workloads
Consider when 'search by keyword/relevance' can't be done efficiently with plain DB indexes
